1.note: This phrase is used here to mark an important event in the story. If your language has a way for doing this, you could consider using it here.
This was a people group from the region of Meun which was near Edom, east of the Jordan River.

1.q: came against Jehoshaphat to do battle
1.note: Here “Jehoshaphat” represents himself and his army. Alternate translation: [came against Jehoshaphat’s army to do battle] or [came to fight against Jehoshaphat and his army]

2.q: See, they are in Hazezon Tamar
2.note: The word “see” is used here as an idiom to add emphasis to what is said next. They could not see the army in Hazezon Tamar from where they were speaking. Alternate translation: [They are already in Hazezon Tamar]
This is the name of a place. It is another name for Engedi.

3.note: This is an idiom. Alternate translation: [determined himself to seek] or [devoted himself to seek]
This speaks of seeking Yahweh’s advice as if he were looking for Yahweh. Alternate translation: [to seek Yahweh’s advice]
The word “fast” can be expressed as a verb. Alternate translation: [He proclaimed that all the people should fast]

4.note: This refers to the people of Judah. Alternate translation: [The people of Judah gathered]

5.note: This refers to the people from these places. Alternate translation: [of the people from Judah and Jerusalem]

6.q: are you not God in heaven? Are you not the ruler over all the kingdoms of the nations?
6.note: Jehoshaphat uses this rhetorical question to emphasize that God is in heaven and his authority over all things. This question can be written as statement. Alternate translation: [you are indeed God in heaven and the ruler over all the kings of the earth.]

6.q: Power and might are in your hand
6.note: The words “Power” and “might” mean basically the same thing and emphasize the greatness of Yahweh’s power. The word “hand” refers to possession. Alternate translation: [You possess great power] or [You have great power and might] (See also: [Synecdoche](ta:figs-synecdoche))

7.q: Our God, did you not drive out the inhabitants of this land … to the descendants of Abraham?
7.note: Jehoshaphat uses this rhetorical question to emphasize that God drove their enemies from their land and gave it to the Israelites. This question can be written as statement. Alternate translation: [It was you who drove out those who lived in this land for the sake of your people Israel and who gave it permanently to the descendants of Abraham.]

8.note: Here Yahweh is represented by his “name.” Alternate translation: [for you] or [to honor you]

9.note: The “sword” represents war. Alternate translation: [war] or [battle]

9.q: your name is in this house
9.note: Here Yahweh’s presence is represented by his “name.” Alternate translation: [your presence is here in this house]

10.note: This was a place where the Edomites lived.

11.q: See how they are rewarding us; they are coming to drive us out of your land
11.note: Here Jehoshaphat speaks of the ironic situation. Alternate translation: [This is how they ‘repay’ us for the mercy we showed to them; they are coming to drive us out of your land]
The word “see” here is used as an idiom to emphasize what is said next.

12.note: This rhetorical question is used as a request. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this question as a statement. Alternate translation: [please judge them.]
Here the people are represented by their “eyes” to emphasize that they are directing their attention to God. Alternate translation: [we are looking to you for help]

14.q: the Spirit of Yahweh came on
14.note: This is an idiom which means that the spirit of God influenced Jahaziel and enabled him to prophesy. See how you translated this in [2 Chronicles 15:1](ta:15)

14.q: Jahaziel … Zechariah … Benaiah … Jeiel … Mattaniah … Asaph
14.note: These are the names of men.

15.q: all Judah and you inhabitants of Jerusalem
15.note: Here “Judah” refers to the people who live there. Alternate translation: [all you who live in Judah and Jerusalem]

15.q: for the battle does not belong to you, but to God
15.note: This means that God is in control of the battle and of what happens.

16.note: This is an idiom that means to go and meet the enemy army for battle. Alternate translation: [march against] or [go to battle against]
Alternate translation: [Pay attention, because what I am about to say is both true and important]
This is a narrow valley between two mountains southeast of Jerusalem.

17.note: This is an idiom that means to go and meet the enemy army for battle. Alternate translation: [March out against] or [Go to battle against]

17.q: the rescue of Yahweh with you
17.note: The word “rescue” can be expressed as a verb. Alternate translation: [Yahweh rescue you]
Here these places represent the people from them. Alternate translation: [people of Judah and Jerusalem]

18.q: bowed his head with his face to the ground … fell down before Yahweh
18.note: These acts of worship that express humility and submission to God.
Here “Judah” refers to the people from Judah. Alternate translation: [All the people of Judah]

19.note: These are the names of people groups descending from Kohath and Korah.
This speaks of all the people praising Yahweh as if they together had one voice. Alternate translation: [with very loud voices]

20.note: Translate the name of this city the same as in 2 Chronicles 11:6.

If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [he will support you] or [he will help you]

20.q: Trust in his prophets, and you will succeed
20.note: Alternate translation: [If you trust in Yahweh’s prophets, then you will succeed]

21.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea behind the word **faithfulness**, you can express the same idea with a verbal form such as “faithfully” or “faithful.” See how you translated “covenant faithfulness” in 2 Chronicles 7:3. Alternate translation: [he faithfully loves us forever] or [he is always faithful to his covenant with us]

22.note: They were singing to Yahweh. Alternate translation: [to sing and to praise Yahweh]
This means that Yahweh caused some of the enemy soldiers to ambush other enemy soldiers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh set some enemy soldiers]
Translate the name of this place the same as in 2 Chronicles 20:10.

If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [They defeated them] or [They defeated those they had ambushed]

23.q: to completely kill them and destroy them
23.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second intensifies the first. Alternate translation: [to completely annihilate them]
This refers to after they had destroyed them. Alternate translation: [When they had finished killing]

24.note: The word “behold” is used here to mark a surprising event.

24.q: they were dead, fallen to the ground
24.note: The phrase “fallen to the ground” is an idiomatic way to say that “they were dead.” Alternate translation: [they were all dead on the ground] (See also: [Doublet](ta:figs-doublet))

26.note: This is the name of a place.
This means the day on which the writer wrote. See how you translated this in 2 Chronicles 5:9.

27.q: every man of Judah and Jerusalem
27.note: This is a reference to every man in the army. Alternate translation: [every soldier of Judah and Jerusalem]
“with Jehoshaphat leading them.” The phrase “in their lead” is an idiom. King Jehoshaphat was in front of the whole army as they went back to Jerusalem.
They rejoiced because their enemies had been defeated. Alternate translation: [rejoice over their enemies’ defeat] or [rejoice because their enemies had been destroyed]

29.q: The terror of God was on all the kingdoms of the nations
29.note: The word “terror” can be expressed with the verb “feared.” Alternate translation: [All the kingdoms of the nations greatly feared God]
Alternate translation: [kingdoms in the nearby nations]

30.note: This speaks of the kingdom having peace as the kingdom being quiet. Alternate translation: [Jehoshaphat’s kingdom was at peace]

31.note: “Azubah” was the name of Jehoshaphat’s mother. Shilhi was the name of Azubah’s father.

32.q: He walked in the ways of Asa, his father; he did not turn away from them
32.note: This means that he lived in a way that pleased Yahweh as his father had done. Here “walking” is an idiom for the way a person lives and behaves. Alternate translation: [He did things that were pleasing to Yahweh, like his father Asa had done, and he did not stop doing those things] (See also: [Idiom](ta:figs-idiom))

32.q: he did what was right in the eyes of Yahweh
32.note: The eyes here represent seeing, and seeing represents judgment. Yahweh saw and approved of Jehoshaphat’s actions. See how you translated a similar phrase in 2 Chronicles 14:2. Alternate translation: [he did what Yahweh judged to be right] or [he did what Yahweh considered to be right]

33.q: the high places were not taken away
33.note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [he did not get rid of the high places]

33.q: The people still had not directed their hearts to the God
33.note: This means that the people did not desire to obey God and were not devoted to him. Here people’s “hearts” represent their will and their desires. Alternate translation: [The people were still not devoted to the God] or [The people still were not committed to following the God]

34.note: These two opposites are given to refer to everything concerning Jehoshaphat during his reign as king. Alternate translation: [from the beginning of his reign until he died]

34.q: behold, they are written in the history … Israel
34.note: The word “behold” is used here to add emphasis to the important information that follows. Alternate translation: [anyone can look in the history … Israel and see that they are written there]

34.q: they are written in … which is recorded in
34.note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they are in … which is in]
Translate this man’s name as you did in 2 Chronicles 16:7.

34.q: the history of Jehu son of Hanani
34.note: This is a historical account that was written by Jehu.

34.q: the book of the kings of Israel
34.note: This is a book that no longer exists. See how you translated this in 2 Chronicles 16:11.

36.note: These are ships capable of traveling on large bodies of water.
This is the name of a city.
Jehoshaphat and Ahaziah did not build the ships, rather, their workers built them. Alternate translation: [Their workers built the ships]
Translate the name of this place as you did in 2 Chronicles 8:17.

37.note: Translate this man’s name as you did in 2 Chronicles 11:8.

37.q: The ships were wrecked so that
37.note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [The ships became ruined and] or [The ships wrecked so that]

37.q: they were not able to sail
37.note: Alternate translation: [no one was able to sail them]
